newsitem.title: UK: U.S. firms to buy Yorkshire Electricity of Britain.
newsitem.headline: U.S. firms to buy Yorkshire Electricity of Britain.

text.p: Ohio-based American Electric Power Co. Inc. and Public Service Co. of Colorado said Monday they planned to buy Yorkshire Electricity Group Plc of Britain for 1.5 billion British pounds ($2.43 billion).
The two U.S. utilities said they expected the acquisition of one of Britain's last independent regional electricity companies to create synergies in power supply, technology and power generation.
If approved, the British utility would be bought by Yorkshire Holdings, a firm owned equally by the two U.S. companies, they said.

The deal, the seventh acquisition of a British utility by an American company, leaves Southern Electric Plc as Britian's only remaining independent regional electricity company of the 12 that were privatised in 1990.
"Yorkshire is particularly attractive to us because of its tradition of low-cost, high-customer service," American Electric Chairman Linn Draper told reporters in a telephone conference call.
Yorkshire said it would not contest the bid as it saw no competitive advantage to staying independent.

"We always said that if somebody came along and offered us a sufficiently high price, and a good deal for our shareholders, we would consider it. And we think this is a very fair price," Yorkshire Chairman Christopher Hampson said.
American Electric, which is based in Columbus, Ohio, and Denver-based Public Service of Colorado said they expected to receive British regulatory clearance for the deal before the end of May.

"If you look at the timelines that have been experienced by other transactions, that would say that there's a high likelihood that it might occur before the election," Draper said, adding that he did not expect the bid to run into problems with regulatory authorities.

However, some analysts questioned the companies' timing, coming just before a national election in Britain, noting that the favoured Labour Party is expected to be less amenable to clearing such an acquisition if it wins the election.

The ruling Conservative Party government already has nodded through bids for 10 of the 12 regional electricity companies. But Labour, ahead in current opinion polls, has proposed a windfall tax on utilities and criticised so-called "fat-cat" pay awards for senior management of the companies.

"Financially, for shareholders, it looks a fair offer," said SocGen analyst Marshall Whiting. "(But) not everybody thinks it's going to go through ... That's what the (share) price is saying to us," he added.
After the announcement, Yorkshire's shares surged 60.5 pence (98 cents) to 879 pence ($14.25) but stayed below the offer price of about 927 pence ($15.03).
The offer represented a premium of 13.3 percent to Yorkshire's closing price Friday and a multiple of 11.3 times the company's earnings, before exceptional items, for the year ended last March 31.
The U.S. utilities said they expect the deal to immediately add to their earnings and that they did not foresee restructuring charges from the transaction.
They also said they expect to reap unspecified cost savings from the deal, which would be a leveraged transaction composed of 75 percent debt and 25 percent equity.
The two U.S. companies said they planned to expand Yorkshire's electricity generation activities in Britain.
They also expect to benefit from Yorkshire's experience when Britain opens up the electricity supply market in 1998.
"We think that we will learn from that," Draper said. "We are actively involved in trying to promote customer choice in our (U.S.) service area."

American Electric and Public Service of Colorado said they had considered other possible acquisitions in Britain and elsewhere abroad, including the only other remaining British independent regional electricity company, Southern Electric Plc .
But the companies said they did not contact Southern officials and did not give further details.
When asked about job cuts, company officials said the fact that Yorkshire's management would be retained boded well for the rest of the utility's workforce.
However, they stopped short of pledging that they would not make job cuts at Yorkshire, noting that the management would continue to evaluate the size of the work force.
Public Service of Colorado's stock added $1 to $39.875 in early afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, while American Electric's stock added 50 cents to $42.375.
